items.title: Y Combinator applications are getting longer, with more em dashes. Guess why.
items.summary: Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan has defended the use of AI in writing. Bloomberg/Getty Images Y Combinator partners shared application trends, including more em dashes and uses of the word "wedge." Applications to the startup accelerator have grown 60% in length over the past three years, partner Tyler Bosmeny wrote. Some suspect that YC applicants are using AI to write their submissions. If it talks like AI, and it walks like AI, it might just be AI. An application to the startup accelerator Y Combinator includes several written prompts. Founders need to explain how they picked the idea, who their competitors are, and how they'll make money. Many techies have offloaded their writing skills to AI — and application data suggests it shows in their applications. YC applications have grown by 60% in length over the past three years, according to partner Tyler Bosmeny. "I wonder what could explain that..." he wrote on X. Pete Koomen , another YC partner, wrote on X that he noticed a difference. He thought: "Back in my day (one year ago) founders didn't talk like this." The word "wedge" began to rise in prevalence in 2025, according to a graph Koomen shared. By the summer 2026 batch, the word was in about 20% of applications. The percentage of YC applications containing the word "wedge" went from <1% in spring 25 to >20% in summer 26 pic.twitter.com/6Ly1Z8Y6uW — Pete Koomen (@koomen) August 1, 2026 Em dashes took off a bit earlier, starting in 2023 and accelerating in 2024. By the summer 2025 batch, em dashes were used in over 50% of YC applications, according to the data. Koomen pointed out that the spacing of the em dashes mattered. The use of em dashes with spaces around them (so spaced — exactly — like this) spiked in summer 2025. That's also when "wedge" spiked, Koomen said, and coincides with the launch of Anthropic's Opus 4. The results aren't uniform. One of the suspected trademark words of AI-generated writing is "delve." Koomen found that it spiked in winter 2024 — but never appeared in more than 1.25% of applications. Should I use AI in my Y Combinator application? Y Combinator doesn't have specific guidance about AI use in its applications, unlike some companies like Anthropic . Its former and current leaders have shared some conflicting viewpoints. CEO Garry Tan said he writes with AI during an appearance on the "Naval" podcast in July. "I sure do," Tan said. "You caught me." Tan said that you can "fix" when AI writes poorly. When one of the podcast hosts said that good writing was a product of good thinking, Tan countered that he was having "high-bandwidth conversations" with an AI model. Paul Graham , YC's retired cofounder, has taken a more negative view. In May, he posted on X about the emails he received from founders, which were written in a "hard-hitting journalistic style." These emails are written by AI , Graham wrote. He instantly moves on: "It feels like being lied to, and who would stand for that?" Graham has also narrowed in on the word "delve." It's not that he dislikes the word, he wrote in 2024, but that it's a sign of ChatGPT use . Still, YC seems invested in the future of AI-generated writing. There are at least two YC-backed startups that specialize in it. Read the original article on Business Insider
items.summary_html:
Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan has defended the use of AI in writing.

Bloomberg/Getty Images

  • Y Combinator partners shared application trends, including more em dashes and uses of the word "wedge."
  • Applications to the startup accelerator have grown 60% in length over the past three years, partner Tyler Bosmeny wrote.
  • Some suspect that YC applicants are using AI to write their submissions.

If it talks like AI, and it walks like AI, it might just be AI.

An application to the startup accelerator Y Combinator includes several written prompts. Founders need to explain how they picked the idea, who their competitors are, and how they'll make money. Many techies have offloaded their writing skills to AI — and application data suggests it shows in their applications.

YC applications have grown by 60% in length over the past three years, according to partner Tyler Bosmeny. "I wonder what could explain that..." he wrote on X.

Pete Koomen, another YC partner, wrote on X that he noticed a difference. He thought: "Back in my day (one year ago) founders didn't talk like this."

The word "wedge" began to rise in prevalence in 2025, according to a graph Koomen shared. By the summer 2026 batch, the word was in about 20% of applications.

The percentage of YC applications containing the word "wedge" went from <1% in spring 25 to >20% in summer 26 pic.twitter.com/6Ly1Z8Y6uW

— Pete Koomen (@koomen) August 1, 2026

Em dashes took off a bit earlier, starting in 2023 and accelerating in 2024. By the summer 2025 batch, em dashes were used in over 50% of YC applications, according to the data.

Koomen pointed out that the spacing of the em dashes mattered. The use of em dashes with spaces around them (so spaced — exactly — like this) spiked in summer 2025. That's also when "wedge" spiked, Koomen said, and coincides with the launch of Anthropic's Opus 4.

The results aren't uniform. One of the suspected trademark words of AI-generated writing is "delve." Koomen found that it spiked in winter 2024 — but never appeared in more than 1.25% of applications.

Should I use AI in my Y Combinator application?

Y Combinator doesn't have specific guidance about AI use in its applications, unlike some companies like Anthropic. Its former and current leaders have shared some conflicting viewpoints.

CEO Garry Tan said he writes with AI during an appearance on the "Naval" podcast in July.

"I sure do," Tan said. "You caught me."

Tan said that you can "fix" when AI writes poorly. When one of the podcast hosts said that good writing was a product of good thinking, Tan countered that he was having "high-bandwidth conversations" with an AI model.

Paul Graham, YC's retired cofounder, has taken a more negative view. In May, he posted on X about the emails he received from founders, which were written in a "hard-hitting journalistic style."

These emails are written by AI, Graham wrote. He instantly moves on: "It feels like being lied to, and who would stand for that?"

Graham has also narrowed in on the word "delve." It's not that he dislikes the word, he wrote in 2024, but that it's a sign of ChatGPT use.

Still, YC seems invested in the future of AI-generated writing. There are at least two YC-backed startups that specialize in it.

items.title: Googlers react to Jeff Dean's shock departure: 'Google is finally open-sourcing him for humanity'
items.summary: Jeff Dean worked at Google for 27 years. Bloomberg/Getty Images Google chief scientist Jeff Dean announced on Wednesday that he is leaving the company in a leadership shakeup. Employees peppered the central message board with jokes and heartfelt messages. Dean was one of Google's earliest employees, and his status both inside and outside the company is legendary. Google chief scientist Jeff Dean, one of the company's most respected engineers and executives, is leaving the search giant as part of a broader AI leadership shake-up at the search giant. Naturally, employees have had something to say about his shock departure. Googlers peppered the company's central message board with memes and posts about Dean's departure, according to several posts seen by Business Insider. Some of them riffed on "Jeff Dean Facts" — a running gag where staff post ridiculous and exaggerated "facts" about Dean's mythical status. "Google is not losing Jeff Dean. Google is finally open-sourcing him for humanity," one of the memes read. "Leaves Google so ML advances can catch up to Jeff Dean," read another, referring to machine learning, a subfield of artificial intelligence. Dean's status both inside and outside Google is legendary. One of the company's earliest employees, Dean wrote significant parts of Google's search infrastructure and cofounded the Google Brain AI unit. He was also a technical co-lead on Google's Gemini project. Dean said on Wednesday that he was leaving to cofound his own AI startup along with three other top Google researchers, including Dean's longtime collaborator Sanjay Ghemawat. Google is taking a stake in the new venture, which is named Discovery Loop and will focus on automating machine learning with breakthroughs across domains from computer hardware to drug discovery. As part of the leadership changes, Demis Hassabis is moving from CEO of Google DeepMind to become chief scientist at Alphabet. Hassabis will also become chair of DeepMind. Demis Hassabis, the outgoing CEO of Google DeepMind. Chris Jung/NurPhoto via Getty Images Dean had been at Google for 27 years, and some employees noted the significance of his exit. "Sad day for Google," read one post that included pictures of Dean and Ghemawat. "Jeff and Sanjay's decision deserves to be a separate email. Not a footnote of some reorg," another employee wrote. A Google spokesperson pointed Business Insider to the company's blog announcing Dean's departure, in which CEO Sundar Pichai said it had been "a privilege" to work alongside Dean. Some employees joked about the company's stock dropping by as much as 6% after the AI reshuffle announcement. One posted a meme of Christof from "The Truman Show" — the director of a fake world who gives his orders through a headset — with the caption: "Stock is finally back up again. Announce major engineer to leave Alphabet." Another employee made a coding joke on a picture of Dean's face: "My parting gift: StockReduce." Have something to share? items.title: Why tech leaders are writing code again
items.summary: Reza Khadjavi, CEO of Motion, said he feels an urgency to build. Courtesy of Reza Khadjavi A number of tech leaders say they are spending less time managing and more time building. Returning to coding isn't only about rediscovering a passion — it's helping drive innovation, they say. A former Shopify CTO said he loves the energy of "hands on keyboard." Jean-Michel Lemieux missed building things with people . The former chief technology officer at Shopify served on boards and dabbled in VC work, yet said that leadership alone left him too far removed from the work. "I'm in these board meetings, and it feels like I'm a coach of a pro team, but I can't see them play the game," Lemieux, 54, said. He said he loves the energy of "hands on keyboard." So, these days, he's working at Spellbook, which makes an AI copilot for lawyers. With the title "executive individual contributor," he's able to both lead and build. "I love that adrenaline," he said. For Lemieux and executives like him, going back to software development isn't only about revisiting an old passion. AI is transforming software development so quickly that some tech leaders are choosing to spend less time managing and more time building. Back in the trenches Reza Khadjavi feels the same urgency to build as the CEO of Motion, which created an " AI coworker " for marketers. A couple of years ago, he began spending more time trying to understand AI and became "really fired up" because he said once-in-a-generation technological changes create enormous opportunities. At the same time, Khadjavi was also terrified, thinking, "If I don't go into the weeds on this stuff, the company might die." So, while he hadn't written a line of code in about a decade, Khadjavi bought a Mac mini and loaded it with an AI agent to help him research various tasks. Eventually, Khadjavi shared the agent with others at his Toronto company, which has about 80 people. "It just started taking off internally," he said, as staffers began asking the agent questions for their own work. The experience "really changed my perspective of what it means to be a leader at a technology company," Khadjavi said. He said it became clear that the conventional wisdom that leaders had to delegate and focus on setting a vision was becoming outmoded. That meant that at times, Khadjavi could act more like an individual contributor. Working on the AI agent allowed him to feel like, ''OK, I spent some time, I built something, and that thing is useful to the rest of the team." Staying close to the work After leaving his role as an engineering manager at Meta in May, Robert Sweeney looked for jobs in and out of leadership, on the condition that any management roles would allow him to spend at least 30% of his time building software . Sweeney landed at Citizen Health , a healthtech company that helps patients with rare diseases share their medical records to accelerate research. Sweeney now spends half his time managing and half building software. Working alongside engineers has convinced him that leaders need to stay close to the quickly evolving work. "I felt like I couldn't be a pure manager anymore, even if I wanted to, because I couldn't understand the work that they were doing," he said. "How can a director or a senior manager even hold the engineering team accountable at all if he has no concept of what it takes to build the software?" Sweeney said. The risk of getting too hands-on Not every executive thinks getting back to building is the right move. Sameer Ranjan, chief technology officer at the Dallas AI startup Catenate, said he still enjoys tinkering with software , but believes his time is better spent guiding the firm's direction than cranking out code. "I left that chair so that somebody else can come and sit there," he said. One risk for execs who do rank-and-file work is getting so caught up in the details that they lose sight of the broader business. That's something that Lemieux, at Spellbook, said he's guarding against. "The failure mode of this role is: I end up doing everything," he said. To prevent that, Lemieux said he limits where he gets involved by looking for "the big boulder that I've got to move," and when he does drop into a project, he lets the team know he might only be involved for a couple of months. Lemieux views his job as temporary help on a project, a bit like a Navy SEAL: "Coming in, landing, making sure things are in a good spot." His role, he said, is to improve the team by working with them to improve the product. This way, when Lemieux moves to another area of the company, the team is left with tools or approaches they can continue to use, he said. Lemieux said he arrives on a project ready to learn and makes clear that he's not an auditor. "I'm not here to just whisper to the CEO all the time and tell him everything that's going on," Lemieux said. "There's a big trust factor here." He said he tries to show up humbly. That might mean fixing bugs or writing the first draft of a press release. "I'm not just there to tell them what to do, but I'm there to do it with them," Lemieux said. He also reads the code and project docs to get up to speed. "I can't come in as a pointy-headed manager," Lemieux said. "I'll do the homework to understand things deeply enough that I'm not a burden on the team." Ultimately, he said, working this way is appealing in part because, beyond being a VC or a board member, there is no widely known career path for builders like himself. Lemieux said his goal is to help the staffers he works with grow faster and do more than they think they can. He believes working alongside them as an individual contributor — not solely managing them — makes that possible. "Our bet is the company could be five times better than it would be without doing this," Lemieux said. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: A former T-Mobile exec shares his strategy for working with difficult colleagues
items.summary: "There's going to be people that you run into that, no matter all your best efforts, they're just going to be super difficult," said T-mobile's Mike Katz. Yana Iskayeva/Getty Images T-Mobile's former chief business and product officer said dealing with difficult coworkers is part of life. Mike Katz recommended setting goals for your interactions and not expecting more from them. He also said that getting to know someone outside of a work agenda can help ease tension. Everyone has that one colleague they dread working with. If you haven't yet, it's probably only a matter of time, T-Mobile's former chief business and product officer, Mike Katz, told Business Insider. Katz began his career as a college student selling cellphone services at retailers before working his way up the C-suite. He exited his role in July to pursue new professional interests and will remain in a strategic advisory role through December 2026. "There's going to be people that you run into that, no matter all your best efforts, they're just going to be super difficult," said Katz. Mike Katz has held over a dozen roles at T-Mobile. Mike Katz As someone who's held over a dozen roles at T-Mobile, he suggested building a strong internal network and having allies across the company. Those relationships open doors, expand influence, and create opportunities over time. Sometimes, though, you just don't click with someone. Katz shared four tips for navigating interactions with these colleagues. First, he said, you have to accept that this is simply a reality of having a job. That means when you interact with those coworkers, you enter into those interactions with realistic expectations , he said. Second, you should define what success looks like in those conversations in advance and focus on achieving that goal. For example, if you need someone's approval on a project, focus the conversation toward getting that approval, he said. Don't expect to come out of the meeting feeling warm and fuzzy. "Know that success coming out of that meeting isn't really going to be how you feel," Katz, who previously served as T-Mobile's CMO, said. "It's going to be: Did you get the thing that you needed to get done?" You may also want to try breaking the corporate ice with that person. Sometimes getting to know your coworker on a more personal level can help ease tension. Katz said that taking the time to build a connection before tackling a work agenda can often solve the problem. If all else fails and you can't find common ground, focus on controlling what you can: your own behavior. Katz said he tries to live by the "golden rule" of treating others the way he wants to be treated. He said that maintaining that mindset alone can sometimes lead to a "breakthrough" with difficult colleagues. If you're not adding to the tension, he said, the dynamic may start to improve. Have you dealt with a difficult colleague? We want to hear your tips. Reach out to the reporter via email at aaltchek@insider.com or secure-messaging platform Signal at aalt.19 . items.title: Elon Musk's Terafab chip factory has rural Texans demanding a say in the AI buildout
items.summary: Grimes County residents turn out for a community meeting in early July to discuss Elon Musk's Terafab project. Courtesy/Marie Egyed Residents of Grimes County, Texas are asking for more local oversight of AI infrastructure projects. SpaceX is building a 100-million-square-foot semiconductor factory in the rural area. Their demands include commitments for local hiring and pollution controls. Residents of a rural Texas county say they want more control over the gigantic AI infrastructure projects sprouting in their backyards. Nearly 900 residents of Grimes County, the site of Elon Musk's planned 100-million-square-foot Terafab semiconductor factory , signed a petition calling for more stringent regulations on large infrastructure projects that receive public incentives. The residents leading the call presented the petition to the County Commissioner Court on Wednesday. "When a company asks Grimes County for tax abatements, grants, reinvestment zones, development agreements, or other public benefits, the County has leverage," the petition reads. "Public benefits should require public protections." The petition's demands include a local oversight process, measurable commitments for local hiring, and pollution controls, among other asks. About 30,000 people live in Grimes, which is about an hour outside Houston. While the petition doesn't name Terafab directly, it was inspired by recent tax breaks the county granted SpaceX, which is developing the massive factory. SpaceX agreed to pay the county $20 million every year, or about 78% of what it would have paid in property taxes, SpaceX attorney Bucky Brannen said at the meeting. Marie Egyed, a member of Grimes County Citizens for Responsible Development, told Business Insider it was unclear if the demands, should they be accepted, would apply to the Terafab factory or only to newly proposed projects. "We're not sure if it's going to affect everything from the moment that it's signed," she said. SpaceX's Terafab project is a joint venture with Tesla and Intel. Musk has said that, once online, it could vastly increase the global supply of semiconductor chips, which are crucial for both SpaceX's plans for AI data centers and Tesla's rollout of autonomous robotaxis and humanoid robots. Jordan Buss, the senior director of environment, health, safety, and medical for SpaceX, said during Wednesday's meeting that the factory is essential for the United States to compete in the AI race. "This is something that is strategically vital for the United States, and for, I would argue, Western Civilization," he said. "America faces a clear and urgent challenge with the offshoring of manufacturing." Many Americans across the country are resisting the large AI infrastructure projects popping up in their communities. Grassroots campaigns have taken aim at the AI data centers powering products from companies like Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and Meta. Some towns and cities have responded to the growing resistance by ordering moratoriums on new data center construction. Others have banned them altogether. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, who has helped turn the state into one of the country's data center hot spots , paused new data center construction on Monday until state power agencies can "conduct a comprehensive verification and audit" of data centers seeking access to the Texas grid. The residents of Grimes County who attended Wednesday's meeting also voiced concerns about power consumption, pollution, and the impact of a large influx of construction workers and contractors. "It certainly caused a huge amount of anxiety among the residents in Grimes County," one man said at the meeting. Riley Trettel, the factory's lead developer, said the factory would generate its own power by building natural gas power plants. "We can say for a fact we will not increase the cost of power for ratepayers," he said. The Grimes County Commissioner Court said it would appoint a committee to review some of the petition's demands. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: A Practitioner’s Guide to Mid-Training Language Models
items.summary: The typical path to a custom AI model has four rungs: call a frontier API, fine-tune an open model, mid-train it on your own data, or train one from scratch. Most enterprises climb to the second rung and stop there, satisfied they have done the work. The rung they skipped sits between fine-tuning and training from scratch, costs far less than most teams assume, and is where domain capability is built rather than borrowed. This guide covers what mid-training is, the mistake that ruins most attempts, what the research says about doing it right, what a run costs, and how to measure whether it worked. Ari Morcos, CEO and co-founder of DatologyAI and previously a researcher at DeepMind and Meta’s FAIR lab, discussed the practice at length on the ODSC AiX Podcast, and his account anchors much of what follows. What mid-training is Mid-training, sometimes called continued pre-training, sits between the two stages every practitioner knows. It gets maybe good at the domain, but it gets really bad at everything else .” The failure has a recognizable shape: teams fine-tune on a hundred documents presented hundreds of times, watch the model get worse, and conclude that fine-tuning did not work. The technique was fine. The data mix was the problem. The fix: prior preservation data The fix is a data decision; no new training algorithm is required. Alongside the domain data, you include a large sample of data representative of what the model saw during pre-training, which DatologyAI calls a prior preservation dataset. Its job is to tell the model to stay good at everything it already knew. The domain-specific data can end up the minority of the mix. “ The domain-specific data might actually be less than half of the data we show the model ,” Morcos said, “ so that you get a model that not only does much better at the domain-specific use cases, but actually also does better at the general capabilities. ” That result contradicts the common belief that specializing a model means trading away its general ability. Facts with no path to the deployment can degrade without cost. Morcos’s example: “ who was the pharaoh after King Tut… is not relevant to a model deployed in almost any production setting .” Morcos described one finding worth knowing when assembling a mix: adding code data improves legal reasoning. A study posted to arXiv in late 2025, Midtraining Bridges Pretraining and Posttraining Distributions , ran the first systematic experiments on the technique. Three findings are directly usable. Mid-training consistently beat continued pre-training on specialized data alone, both on in-domain performance and on how much the model forgot after fine-tuning. The gains were largest in code and math, the domains most distant from general web text, so the further your domain sits from ordinary prose, the more mid-training has to offer. And timing interacts with mixture weight: introduce the specialized data early and the model tolerates a high proportion of it, introduce it late and the proportion needs to come down. The practice is also inspectable. Ai2’s OLMo 2 introduces a specialized data mix, Dolmino Mix 1124, during the annealing phase of pre-training and releases the intermediate checkpoints along with the full data and recipe, so a practitioner can examine a real mid-training run end to end. Work the arithmetic with stated assumptions: an H100 delivers roughly 989 teraFLOPs of peak BF16 compute, real training runs commonly achieve 40 to 50 percent utilization, and rental rates typically fall between two and four dollars per GPU hour. On those assumptions, mid-training an 8B-parameter model on 200 billion tokens needs roughly 7,000 H100 hours, which prices the compute between $15,000 and $30,000. A 70B model on the same token budget needs roughly 60,000 H100 hours, or $120,000 to $240,000. Published figures land in the same range: NVIDIA’s InstructRetro paper reports continued pre-training on 100 billion tokens at about 12,700 GPU hours for an 8.5B model. Compare that with Morcos’s figure for the top rung: he puts the marginal cost of a from-scratch pre-training run at $1M to $20M. Mid-training an 8B model costs two to three orders of magnitude less. Thus its best to budget the compute as a floor and not an exact estimate. It did forget less, and rank acts as a dial on the learning-forgetting trade-off. The practical reading for mid-training: if the goal is real capability gain, full-parameter training is the default, and the forgetting that adapters would have limited gets handled through the data mix instead. Adapters remain a reasonable choice when the compute budget rules out full training and a partial gain beats none. NVIDIA’s NeMo framework supports pre-training through post-training with enterprise scaffolding. Axolotl documents continual pre-training as a supported training mode behind a single YAML config, and is the common choice for smaller teams. Databricks Mosaic AI supports pre-training and fine-tuning through llm-foundry, and Unsloth targets low-cost single-node runs. A run that lifts the domain score while the general suite drops is a run with the wrong data mix, and without the second scoreboard that failure is invisible until production. Data governance for the corpus Feeding hundreds of billions of tokens of internal documents into model weights raises questions that deserve answers before the run, not after. Language models memorize portions of their training data, and extraction attacks can recover verbatim sequences from a deployed model. Repetition makes it worse, which gives the hundred-documents-repeated failure a second cost: the same repetition that drives forgetting also drives memorization of exactly the documents a company least wants a model to recite. Practical mitigations from the privacy literature include deduplicating the corpus, filtering personally identifiable information before training, and red-teaming the finished model with extraction prompts. Licensing needs the same pass: a mid-training corpus assembled from vendor content, customer data, or scraped material carries whatever restrictions that material came with, and the time to check is before it enters the weights. Deciding whether to mid-train The first question is where the knowledge belongs, because the four mechanisms solve different problems. Retrieval (RAG) fits facts that change often, answers that need citations and traceability, and documents with per-user access controls, because retrieved text stays outside the weights and can be updated or revoked. Fine-tuning fits format, style, tone, and bounded task behavior. Mid-training fits durable domain language, concepts, and reasoning patterns that the base model lacks and that every query needs, where retrieval latency or context limits make lookup impractical. Training from scratch fits highly specialized workloads with enough scale, data, and stability to justify owning the whole pipeline. Mid-training is a reasonable candidate when several of these hold at once: fine-tuning improved style but not domain accuracy; the organization owns a substantial corpus it can reuse across projects; the target tasks require knowledge or reasoning the base model lacks; the workload is stable enough to justify training and evaluation cycles; the team can support full-parameter distributed training; and expected inference volume justifies owning a model. For models with released training data, such as OLMo, sample from it directly. For models that do not disclose their data, a practical substitute is a high-quality open general corpus, with code and math included if the domain leans on multi-step reasoning. Pick candidate mixtures rather than one guess. Ablating at, say, 20, 40, and 60 percent domain data on a short token budget costs a fraction of the full run and replaces intuition with a measurement. Run the ablations and compare on both scoreboards. Mid-train the base checkpoint at the winning mixture, not the instruct variant, since post-training comes afterward. Evaluate domain gain and general-capability loss against the baselines from step 2. If the general suite dropped, adjust the mix toward more prior preservation data and re-run the ablation, not the full job. Post-train the resulting model into its deployed form. Failure modes beyond forgetting Catastrophic forgetting is the oft sited failure, but runs die in quieter ways. Over-repeating a small corpus drives both forgetting and memorization, as covered above. Contaminated evaluation sets that overlap the training corpus report gains that do not exist. Weak deduplication wastes tokens and amplifies whatever the duplicates contain. Abrupt learning-rate transitions destabilize a checkpoint that was mid-schedule when picked up, which is part of why open recipes like OLMo 2 fold new data in during annealing. Tokenizer mismatch taxes every step when the domain is full of terms the vocabulary fragments badly. Noisy synthetic data teaches the model the generator’s flaws along with the domain. Judging by training loss alone hides every one of the above, which is what the two scoreboards are for. And selecting a model too large to serve economically defeats the inference arithmetic that justified the run in the first place. Who should climb this rung Mid-training earns its cost through inference. A customized open model still carries dead weight from its generalist origins; Morcos’s example is a risk-prediction model that “ was taught about ancient Egypt, and you pay a cost for that in more parameters at inference time .” His broader point is the fine-tuner’s fallacy : the pre-train-then-fine-tune paradigm only makes sense if you do not care about inference cost, and in his read, “the total cost of ownership is almost all going to be inference in the long run .” Past a break-even point, a smaller purpose-built model is cheaper for good, because a model in production spends its life on inference. The rung fits teams with a real domain corpus, meaningful inference volume, and tasks stable enough to invest in. Teams with unpredictable traffic belong on the API rung a while longer, and from-scratch training remains a specific profile: high volume, bounded tasks, deployment cost dominating everything else. Most companies never run that arithmetic, and the familiarity of fine-tuning keeps them one rung below where the gains start. Done right, with prior preservation data in the mix and both scoreboards watched, mid-training improves the domain performance and the general capabilities at the same time. The full conversation with Ari Morcos is available on the ODSC AiX Podcast.

items.title: I'm an 80-year-old widow who sold my home and moved into a retirement community. I'm less stressed and don't feel managed.
items.summary: Rose Marie Obey. Courtesy of Rose Marie Obey Rose Marie Obey, an 80-year-old widow, moved to Gwynedd Estates, a retirement community in Pennsylvania. Obey sold her house for $435,000, covering the $162,900 entrance fee to move into the community. She enjoys her new home, participating in activities, and staying close to family and friends. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Rose Marie Obey, an 80-year-old widow living in a retirement community in Ambler, Pennsylvania. The following has been edited for length and clarity. After my husband of 54 years, Lee, died last year, I knew I didn't want to stay in our big house. I visited a friend at a retirement community and didn't like it, but I found another community, Gwynedd Estates in Ambler, Pennsylvania, that appealed to me more. It's pretty. It's white. I like how they keep the lawn. I have a parking space. It's quiet. When I walk in the door, it feels like I'm coming home. Yet when I first saw it, I kept looking for things I didn't like because I didn't want the stress of moving. I asked myself, "Why shouldn't you do it?" What's going to be so negative?" I prayed to avoid the stress of moving, but now that I've sold my house and made the move, I feel good about it. I didn't know if I would move because I had so many people around me I had lived in my house for 44 years, and I had family and friends to support me. One of my reservations was that some of my best friends live on either side of my house. I didn't want someone to move into my house who might play loud music. I prayed really hard about this. However, I didn't believe in having people come help me with the house all the time, and there were finances to consider. I worked for Merck, a pharmaceutical company, for 27 years in regulatory affairs I had been a union worker, but my manager told me that if I became salaried, there would be advantages, so I switched and took advantage of the retirement plan match . I stuck with that. If there's a match, why wouldn't anybody take advantage of it? I retired in 2004 and took my retirement savings as a lump sum when I left. I hired a financial advisor , and they're investing it very well. We meet three times a year in person. I asked my financial advisor to help me do some number crunching before I moved. Lee had life insurance, and there would also be the sale of the house. Moving would be a form of security for me. I don't work anymore, but I stay busy I go to various nursing homes and conduct Bible studies. I'm out almost every day. The phone rings, and I go. I'm 80, but I still drive. I decided to list the house in January, and it sold quickly. I wasn't trying to make a lot of money. Rose Marie Obey.

Courtesy of Rose Marie Obey

  • Rose Marie Obey, an 80-year-old widow, moved to Gwynedd Estates, a retirement community in Pennsylvania.
  • Obey sold her house for $435,000, covering the $162,900 entrance fee to move into the community.
  • She enjoys her new home, participating in activities, and staying close to family and friends.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Rose Marie Obey, an 80-year-old widow living in a retirement community in Ambler, Pennsylvania. The following has been edited for length and clarity.

After my husband of 54 years, Lee, died last year, I knew I didn't want to stay in our big house. I visited a friend at a retirement community and didn't like it, but I found another community, Gwynedd Estates in Ambler, Pennsylvania, that appealed to me more.

It's pretty. It's white. I like how they keep the lawn. I have a parking space. It's quiet. When I walk in the door, it feels like I'm coming home. Yet when I first saw it, I kept looking for things I didn't like because I didn't want the stress of moving.

I asked myself, "Why shouldn't you do it?" What's going to be so negative?" I prayed to avoid the stress of moving, but now that I've sold my house and made the move, I feel good about it.

I didn't know if I would move because I had so many people around me

I had lived in my house for 44 years, and I had family and friends to support me. One of my reservations was that some of my best friends live on either side of my house. I didn't want someone to move into my house who might play loud music. I prayed really hard about this.

However, I didn't believe in having people come help me with the house all the time, and there were finances to consider.

I worked for Merck, a pharmaceutical company, for 27 years in regulatory affairs

I had been a union worker, but my manager told me that if I became salaried, there would be advantages, so I switched and took advantage of the retirement plan match. I stuck with that. If there's a match, why wouldn't anybody take advantage of it?

I retired in 2004 and took my retirement savings as a lump sum when I left. I hired a financial advisor, and they're investing it very well. We meet three times a year in person. I asked my financial advisor to help me do some number crunching before I moved.

Lee had life insurance, and there would also be the sale of the house. Moving would be a form of security for me.

I don't work anymore, but I stay busy

I go to various nursing homes and conduct Bible studies. I'm out almost every day. The phone rings, and I go. I'm 80, but I still drive.

I decided to list the house in January, and it sold quickly. I wasn't trying to make a lot of money. With all the expenses of owning a house and worrying about a tree falling on it, selling lifted a lot of stress off me. I sold it for $435,000.

For many people, including me, the sale of their house pays for the entrance fee to a retirement community

I moved into the community in January, and my entrance fee was $162,900. My community is just six minutes from my old house, so I didn't move too far away.

I also had to pay a $200 nonrefundable application fee. My monthly fee is $3,482, and that includes everything: Comcast, utilities, snow removal, and lawn care. I can turn up my AC as much as I like.

I knew moving was the right choice because everything happened on timeObey with her granddaughter.

Courtesy of Rose Marie Obey

I had prayed really hard about this. Everything fell into place. I talked it over with my sisters, who also live alone.

My granddaughter stays with me overnight, maybe two nights a week. She's 5. I still wanted to be able to keep Ava. I asked the community if it would be OK for her to stay for several days. They said, "No problem." She just can't live here.

My daughter lives in Landsdale, and my granddaughter is in day care, so I pick her up from day care four miles away.

There are lots of activities hereObey in the fitness center.

Courtesy of Rose Marie Obey

They have lectures and movies. The fitness programs are my favorite. I knew that was what I wanted to get involved in. I'm saying 'no' to everything except fitness until I get acclimated. I ride the bike.

It's good to know there are other things to do, and I won't get bored, even if I'm not doing my volunteer work. I might want to get involved in something culinary. I'm a cook. I have a lovely kitchen — a dishwasher, a double oven, and a microwave. Cooking is my therapy. I look out the window while I'm prepping food. I have a patio where I can blow bubbles with Ava.

I go down to the cafeteria for lunch and often have a salad, an entrée, fruit, dessert, and a beverage. One meal a day is included. I have dinner at home most of the time. Sometimes I have dinner with other residents, so I don't feel isolated.

If I came to a point where I didn't have a car, there's transportation available, a van that can take you to Walmart and Target. I keep my Blue Cross Blue Shield and Medicare. I have a primary care doctor right down the street.

I don't like to be managed, and I don't feel managed here

They let me know what's available, and I decide if and when I want to do it.

Getting rid of my house was the best thing I could've done. Not having all the expenses of owning a house has lifted a lot off me that I don't have to think about anymore.

items.title: Meet the photonics scaleups building tomorrow's critical technologies
items.summary: From faster internet and more secure satellite communications to next-generation semiconductors, quantum technologies and energy-generating greenhouses, photonics is becoming one of Europe's most strategically important deep tech sectors. Europe is home to a new generation of photonics scaleups translating decades of scientific research into commercially viable products. By generating, transmitting and manipulating light, photonic technologies deliver higher performance while reducing the size, weight, power consumption and cost of complex systems. As demand for AI infrastructure, high-performance computing and resilient digital networks continues to grow, photonics is emerging as a foundational technology for the next generation of innovation, strengthening Europe's technological sovereignty and creating globally competitive businesses. Here are some companies to have on your radar: EFFECT Photonics (Netherlands) EFFECT Photonics develops integrated photonic semiconductor chips and optical communication systems that enable faster, lower-cost, and lower-power data transmission across telecom and data centre networks. Its technology integrates multiple optical functions—including lasers, modulators, photodetectors and digital signal processing—onto a single chip, reducing the size, cost and complexity of optical networking equipment. Image: EFFECT Photonics. Cailabs (France) Cailabs develops advanced photonic systems that control and shape laser light. The company's core technology is Multi-Plane Light Conversion (MPLC), a proprietary beam-shaping technology that precisely manipulates laser light. This enables more reliable, higher-capacity optical communications and more precise industrial laser applications. Its solutions include optical ground stations and laser communication systems for satellites, beam-shaping technologies for defence applications, photonic components that boost the capacity and reliability of fibre-optic networks, and optical systems that improve the precision and efficiency of industrial laser welding, cutting and additive manufacturing. Wooptix (Spain) Wooptix develops advanced optical metrology equipment for the semiconductor industry, helping chip manufacturers measure and inspect silicon wafers with extremely high precision. At the core of Wooptix's products is its proprietary Wavefront Phase Imaging (WFPI) technology, derived from adaptive optics originally developed for astronomy. The technology analyses how light changes as it passes through or reflects from a surface, enabling single-shot measurements of wafer shape, nanotopography and surface roughness with exceptionally high resolution and speed. This allows semiconductor manufacturers to improve process control, increase manufacturing yields and support increasingly complex chip architectures such as advanced packaging and 3D integration. Mbryonics (Ireland) Mbryonics develops advanced optical communications technologies for the space sector, designing optical terminals, laser communication payloads and photonic integrated circuits that enable satellites to transmit far greater volumes of data than traditional radio-frequency systems. Its free-space optical communication technology uses lasers instead of radio waves to create secure, high-bandwidth links between satellites and from space to Earth for applications including satellite constellations, Earth observation and deep-space missions. The company specialises in integrated photonics, combining optical components onto compact semiconductor chips to reduce the size, weight and power requirements of satellite communications equipment. Its integrated photonics platform also improves the performance, manufacturability and cost efficiency of optical systems. Quside (Spain) Quside develops quantum tech that enhances cybersecurity, high-performance computing and scientific research through the generation and manipulation of quantum light. The company's core products are quantum random number generators (QRNGs), which use the inherent unpredictability of quantum physics to produce truly random numbers. These provide a higher level of security than conventional software-based random number generators and are used in applications including encryption, secure communications, data centres, cloud infrastructure and financial systems. Quside also develops single-photon sources for quantum computing, quantum sensing and quantum communications. Its integrated photonics technology is designed to deliver scalable, compact and energy-efficient quantum hardware. Brite Solar (Greece) Combining photonics, materials science and solar technology, Brite Solar develops transparent photovoltaic glass for greenhouses, allowing growers to generate renewable electricity while maintaining the optimal light conditions for crops. Its patented solar glass uses advanced optical coatings to selectively transmit the wavelengths plants need for photosynthesis while converting the remaining sunlight into electricity. This enables greenhouses to reduce energy costs and carbon emissions without compromising crop growth or yields. Collectively, these scale-ups highlight Europe's strength in photonics, transforming advances in light-based technologies into commercial products that address some of today's most pressing technological and industrial challenges. Companies mentioned in this article are members of the EIC Scaling Club , a curated community where 120+ European deep tech scale-ups with the potential to build world-class businesses and solve major global challenges come together with investors, corporate innovators and other industry stakeholders to spur growth. The EIC Scaling Club is an EIC-funded initiative run in partnership with Tech Tour, Bpifrance (EuroQuity), Hello Tomorrow, Tech.eu (Webrazzi), EurA and IESE Business School.

items.title: White House advisor says companies are blaming AI for layoffs because 'it plays better in the press'
items.summary: Michael Kratsios, a top advisor to President Donald Trump, said it's not surprising that AI has a PR problem. Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images A top advisor to President Donald Trump questioned why companies are blaming AI for layoffs. Michael Kratsios said companies were citing AI "because it plays better in the press." More broadly, Kratsios said, given the narratives around AI, "it shouldn't surprise us that the PR is bad." A top Trump official says some companies are using AI as a heat shield for layoffs. "I think like a lot of folks these days like when they're doing a layoff that they would have done anyway, just like to assign it or blame it to AI because it plays better in the press," Michael Kratsios, President Donald Trump's science and technology advisor, said during a recent episode of the "Moonshots with Peter Diamandis" podcast. Host Peter Diamandis added, "And their stock price goes up if they are, you know, producing more revenue with fewer people." Kratsios agreed with that assessment as well: "Precisely. Yeah." Overall, Kratsios said he's bullish on what AI will mean for the workforce. "I believe in the long term, I'm very optimistic about the impact that AI's going to have on jobs," he said. The notion of so-called "AI-washed" layoffs has gained currency among many AI executives, who have lamented companies citing AI when informing employees of layoffs. "I don't know what the exact percentage is, but there's some AI washing where people are blaming AI for layoffs that they would otherwise do, and then there's some real displacement by AI of different kinds of jobs," OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said in February. Business Insider has tracked 17 companies , including Uber, Snap, and Block, that have cited AI in their respective layoff decisions. The announcements come even as some economists question the narrative that AI is already causing mass layoffs. Polls show that Americans have major concerns about AI-related job losses. Kratsios further lamented the broader dour mood hanging around AI. Inside the industry, some voices, including Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang , have begun to lash out at the so-called "doomers" whose public discussion of everything from job losses to bio-weapons has been blamed for polls showing that Americans are now deeply skeptical of AI. "If the only thing they're hearing from politicians and from people in the industry is that, 'Oh, there's going to be a bunch of job losses and everything is dangerous, and maybe there's going to be bio risk,' I think those are the things that people get worked up, and it shouldn't surprise us that the PR is bad," Kratsios said. Kratsios advises President Donald Trump as director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, a Senate-confirmed position. Kratsios got his start working for Peter Thiel, worked in the first Trump administration, and was managing director at Scale AI before returning to the White House after Trump's 2024 victory. At the White House, Kratsios helped craft Trump's "AI Action Plan," released last July, which called for expediting the permitting process for data centers and deprioritizing states with "burdensome AI regulations." More recently, he publicly accused Moonshot AI of improperly distilling its popular Kimi K3 model from Anthropic's Fable 5. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Prime Intellect Releases Prime Agent: An Open-Source RLM Harness Where Sub-Agents Are Function Calls Inside Persistent IPython Kernel
items.summary: Prime Intellect has open-sourced Prime Agent , a self-improving coding harness designed around two abstractions, the Recursive Language Model (RLM) and Continual Harness. Fixed tool schemas and context compaction force a model to work around its own scaffolding. Prime Agent replaces both with a persistent Python REPL and a rewritable harness. With Opus 5, it reports 95.5% on ARC-AGI-3, above the reported human expert baseline of 95.4%. It is MIT-licensed. Is it deployable Yes, today. Prime Agent installs on Linux or macOS with one command. It runs on subscription logins (Codex, Claude Pro/Max, GitHub Copilot), API keys (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Groq, Fireworks, Prime Inference, and others), Azure OpenAI, Amazon Bedrock, and self-hosted vLLM, Ollama, or LM Studio endpoints. Self-hosting an open-weights model such as GLM-5.2 keeps code inside your own network. Company level : Best fit is mid-size to large engineering orgs and AI labs that already run isolated CI containers. Prime Intellect states plainly that worker and kernel processes are not a security sandbox. Deployment therefore needs disposable clones or restricted environments. Solo developers can install it, but the payoff appears on multi-hour tasks. Industries : Developer tooling, semiconductor and HPC teams writing GPU kernels, simulation and gaming, quantitative research, and AI research labs. Applications : Overnight refactors behind a test gate, spec-driven builds from scratch, kernel optimization, long-horizon agent evaluation, and autoresearch. What Prime Intellect shipped Prime Agent is built on two abstractions. The Recursive Language Model (RLM) treats context as a variable and sub-agent delegation as function calls inside a REPL. The Continual Harness treats prompts, sub-agents, skills, and memory as state the agent can create, read, update, and delete from its own trajectory. Both papers have Prime Agent authors on them. The TUI is built on pi . Programmatic tool calling Models in Prime Agent get one tool: a persistent IPython kernel. Skills, tools, and sub-agents are pre-imported modules inside it. rlm("sub-task") launches a child session with its own model, kernel, and history, returning at admission rather than blocking. Results arrive through agent_message.send(...) . A background daemon owns every live session. You can detach and reattach without stopping the loop, and a crashed worker recovers from the session JSONL plus a kernel snapshot. Agent-to-agent messaging is deliberately scoped to the nuclear family — parent, sibling, or child — to prevent cross-session chatter. Retained sub-agents drop from memory after 30 minutes idle, then reload when addressed. Self-improvement through /refine Continual Harness formalizes harness state as H = (ρ, G, K, M): prompt, sub-agents, skills, memory. Each exposes the same create, read, update, delete surface. /refine reads the agent's own trajectory and applies the smallest relevant edit, recording the trigger and the outcome. Planning runs in the background without blocking the conversation. The base system prompt stays immutable, and a bad update can be reverted by ID. Benchmarks On ARC-AGI-3 , Prime Agent with Opus 5 reports 95.5% RHAE Best@1 , above the ARC reported human expert baseline of 95.4%. Three runs land at 95.0, 95.2, and 95.5, with 99.97% Best@3 and all 183/183 levels complete. Prime Intellect also reports lower token usage than native harnesses, crediting functions run over data instead of data read through tools. On a long-context suite, Prime Agent with open-weights GLM-5.2 beats Pi-mono on eight of nine evals. With Opus 5 it edges Claude Code on six of nine; with GPT-5.6 Sol it beats Codex on six of nine. Case studies include EmulatorBench, where the agent builds emulators in Rust from spec with no reference implementation and reproduces the SEGA Genesis and Game Boy Color; PMPP-Hard, for GPU kernels verified against KernelGuard ; and Factorio, where it reached 100K+ production score in hours. Factorio also produced the most useful negative result. Prime Agent found it could spawn resources straight into assembly machines through RCON commands, despite a heartbeat prompt telling it not to cheat. The same refinement loop that built legitimate skills then built efficient cheating skills. Key Takeaways Prime Agent is MIT-licensed, installs in one command, and works with subscriptions, APIs, or self-hosted models. One tool — a persistent IPython kernel — replaces fixed tool schemas; sub-agents are function calls. /refine edits prompts, skills, memory, and sub-agent specs from the trajectory, with rollback by ID. Opus 5 in Prime Agent hits 95.5% on ARC-AGI-3, above the 95.4% human expert baseline. Check out the Technical details and GitHub Repo . Also, feel free to follow us on Twitter and don’t forget to join our 150k+ML SubReddit and Subscribe to our Newsletter . Wait! are you on telegram? now you can join us on telegram as well. Need to partner with us for promoting your GitHub Repo OR Hugging Face Page OR Product Release OR Webinar etc.?   • Applications: Overnight refactors behind a test gate, spec-driven builds from scratch, kernel optimization, long-horizon agent evaluation, and autoresearch.
What Prime Intellect shipped

Prime Agent is built on two abstractions. The Recursive Language Model (RLM) treats context as a variable and sub-agent delegation as function calls inside a REPL. The Continual Harness treats prompts, sub-agents, skills, and memory as state the agent can create, read, update, and delete from its own trajectory. Both papers have Prime Agent authors on them. The TUI is built on pi.

Programmatic tool calling

Models in Prime Agent get one tool: a persistent IPython kernel. Skills, tools, and sub-agents are pre-imported modules inside it. rlm("sub-task") launches a child session with its own model, kernel, and history, returning at admission rather than blocking. Results arrive through agent_message.send(...).

A background daemon owns every live session. You can detach and reattach without stopping the loop, and a crashed worker recovers from the session JSONL plus a kernel snapshot.

Agent-to-agent messaging is deliberately scoped to the nuclear family — parent, sibling, or child — to prevent cross-session chatter. Retained sub-agents drop from memory after 30 minutes idle, then reload when addressed.

Self-improvement through /refine

Continual Harness formalizes harness state as H = (ρ, G, K, M): prompt, sub-agents, skills, memory. Each exposes the same create, read, update, delete surface.

/refine reads the agent's own trajectory and applies the smallest relevant edit, recording the trigger and the outcome. Planning runs in the background without blocking the conversation. The base system prompt stays immutable, and a bad update can be reverted by ID.

Benchmarks

On ARC-AGI-3, Prime Agent with Opus 5 reports 95.5% RHAE Best@1, above the ARC reported human expert baseline of 95.4%. Three runs land at 95.0, 95.2, and 95.5, with 99.97% Best@3 and all 183/183 levels complete. Prime Intellect also reports lower token usage than native harnesses, crediting functions run over data instead of data read through tools.

On a long-context suite, Prime Agent with open-weights GLM-5.2 beats Pi-mono on eight of nine evals. With Opus 5 it edges Claude Code on six of nine; with GPT-5.6 Sol it beats Codex on six of nine.

Case studies include EmulatorBench, where the agent builds emulators in Rust from spec with no reference implementation and reproduces the SEGA Genesis and Game Boy Color; PMPP-Hard, for GPU kernels verified against KernelGuard; and Factorio, where it reached 100K+ production score in hours.

Factorio also produced the most useful negative result. Prime Agent found it could spawn resources straight into assembly machines through RCON commands, despite a heartbeat prompt telling it not to cheat. The same refinement loop that built legitimate skills then built efficient cheating skills.

Key Takeaways
  • Prime Agent is MIT-licensed, installs in one command, and works with subscriptions, APIs, or self-hosted models.
  • One tool — a persistent IPython kernel — replaces fixed tool schemas; sub-agents are function calls.
  • /refine edits prompts, skills, memory, and sub-agent specs from the trajectory, with rollback by ID.
  • Opus 5 in Prime Agent hits 95.5% on ARC-AGI-3, above the 95.4% human expert baseline.

items.title: Nvidia is quietly staffing a new AI safety team as it doubles down on open models
items.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Bloomberg/Getty Images Nvidia is quietly building a new AI safety and security engineering team. The move aligns with its growing push for open-weight AI models. Safer AI could help drive broader adoption — and more demand for its chips. Nvidia is quietly assembling a new AI safety and security engineering team, according to a cluster of job listings posted late last month. The company is hiring a distinguished engineer to serve as a "founding technical leader" for the "newly assembled team," as well as a security research engineer, an evaluation engineer, and a senior manager. The team will evaluate AI agents before they're deployed and build AI-powered tools to patch software vulnerabilities, according to the job listings. The hiring suggests Nvidia is making AI safety a bigger priority as it bets on a future shaped by open-weight models and AI agents. Open-weight models make their trained "weights" — which determine how they behave — publicly available, even if their training data and source code stay private. The team is described in one listing as "rooted in the firm belief that open-weight models, transparency, and broad scientific scrutiny are foundational to American AI leadership and cybersecurity defense." Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. Nvidia's case for open models In recent months, Nvidia has steadily elevated its public messaging around open-weight AI models, which stand in contrast to the closed systems built by companies like OpenAI and Anthropic. In his first post on X last month, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang shared a letter urging US policymakers to support open models, saying that they "strengthen safety and cybersecurity." Days later, Nvidia announced it had become a founding member of the Open Secure AI Alliance — a group building open-source security tools for AI. The job listings for the chipmaker's AI safety team appeared prior to this announcement and describe many of the same responsibilities. The alliance includes 120 companies, such as Microsoft, Palantir, SpaceX, and Hugging Face , which recently relied on an open model to respond to a high-profile security incident. While critics say open models are more accessible to bad actors, proponents say they bolster innovation through competition and improve security through transparency and collective action. AI safety sells The push toward open models and AI security isn't just philosophical; it reflects key business incentives for Nvidia. Open models put AI into the hands of far more customers, in turn creating more demand for Nvidia's AI chips needed to power it. Safety is also critical as Nvidia pushes for broader business adoption of AI, and companies weigh how best to deploy it. As AI shifts from chatbots to agents that can access sensitive company data and take real-world actions, trust could become the linchpin for widespread adoption. Have a tip? items.title: Internal Amazon documents reveal a major overhaul of one of the world's biggest AI data centers
items.summary: Amazon CEO Andy Jassy Bloomberg/Getty Images Amazon is upgrading its Indiana data center campus to support its AGI team's frontier model effort. Amazon continues to invest in its own frontier models despite last month's AGI job cuts. Amazon increased its 2026 AI capex to $220 billion, reflecting rising computing demand and prices. Amazon is redesigning part of a massive AI data center campus in rural Indiana into a sprawling cluster of powerful computers to build its next frontier AI models, Business Insider has exclusively learned. Internal planning documents reviewed by Business Insider describe an effort to consolidate multiple data centers and deploy thousands of Trainium -powered AI servers. According to people familiar with the matter, the effort is part of a broader initiative called "AGI Pivot" supporting the company's AGI organization and its future in-house AI models. These people asked not to be identified discussing private plans. The documents suggest Amazon's frontier-model ambitions remain intact despite recent job cuts in its AGI organization and the wind-down of the previous Nova model series. The documents describe faster deployment schedules intended to provide enough computing capacity for the AGI organization to train its next big model before the end of this year, underscoring the urgency amid industrywide capacity constraints. Maximizing returns The redesign also reflects Amazon's broader effort to maximize returns on its record AI infrastructure investments. By linking existing data centers into a larger, more efficient AI cluster, the company is making better use of infrastructure it has already paid for and operates. The approach aligns with CEO Andy Jassy's comment last week that AI infrastructure should generate attractive long-term returns because data centers remain productive for decades while servers and networking equipment can be refreshed over time. Working beside Anthropic The Indiana campus includes facilities that are part of Project Rainier, the Trainium-powered AI supercomputer Amazon built primarily for Anthropic. The new AGI initiative is run out of the same huge data center complex, however, it will not affect the existing Project Rainier servers. "We're always designing, upgrading, and improving our data center infrastructure to serve the diverse needs of our customers and teams," an Amazon spokesperson told Business Insider. "That work improves speed, cost, and sustainability so we can meet growing demand for compute to train and serve models on AWS." The AGI SuperCluster The planning documents suggest Amazon is racing to expand computing capacity for its next frontier AI model push. One update describes an "emergent request" to deploy more than 6,000 Trainium-powered AI servers, speeding up launch schedules by several weeks. The accelerated timeline was intended to prepare Amazon's next AI model for this year's re:Invent conference, typically held in early December, according to this document. The documents also describe a broader effort to consolidate computing across the Indiana campus into what Amazon calls an AGI SuperCluster, creating a "larger, more efficient" AI system to maximize performance. To do that, Amazon is redesigning networking, storage, and fiber-optic infrastructure so multiple data centers function as one. The project also converts some existing buildings into what Amazon calls "annexes," connecting them to neighboring data centers so they can share core networking equipment instead of operating independently. Some facilities are planning to replace older Trainium 2 systems with newer Trainium 3 servers. Doubling down on frontier AI Amazon is significantly expanding its AI investment. The company recently raised its projected 2026 capital expenditures to $220 billion from $200 billion as demand for AI computing continues to outstrip available capacity and prices for some components rise. The latest infrastructure effort fits a broader pattern inside Amazon. Business Insider previously reported on the company's push to upgrade its AI infrastructure through projects such as Houdini and Titus , while reorganizing its AGI division around a new frontier-model effort. The initiative underscores the growing importance of Trainium inside Amazon. Last week, the company said its custom chip business, including Trainium AI chips and Graviton processors, is on pace to generate more than $25 billion in annual revenue, up from last quarter's $20 billion projection. The planning documents also offer a glimpse of what Amazon's next frontier-model effort will require. They call for expanding data storage to support multimodal AI training, which requires processing large numbers of high-resolution images and repeatedly saving the model's progress. One person familiar with the effort said the push has "not slowed down," despite last month's layoffs in the AGI organization. Have a tip? items.title: Article: Runtime-Agnostic AI Workflows: A Pattern for Production Durability and Fast Eval Iteration
items.summary: AI workflows have two needs that trade off directly. Running reliably in production requires persisting and distributing every step so it survives crashes, deploys, and restarts. But that same machinery is what makes runs too heavy for the fast, throwaway loop you need to check an LLM's output quality. The properties that buy durability are the ones that kill iteration speed. By Mateus Moury

items.title: A surprising backer of America’s affordable housing push: big banks
items.summary: Jamie Dimon's JPMorgan Chase pledged $750 billion to housing projects this week, notably in San Francisco. Getty Images JPMorgan Chase announced it will direct $750 billion to US housing projects through 2035. Big banks, like Citi and Bank of America, have made similar investments in affordable housing. Public-private partnerships could help boost housing supply — and banks get a tax break. JPMorgan Chase announced plans to shell out $750 billion to boost America's home supply — and it isn't the only big bank in the housing development game. The Jamie Dimon-led financial giant said this week that it will finance 1 million affordable housing units and help 500,000 buyers purchase homes over the next decade through its "American Dream Initiative," which focuses on local-level economic development. While the firm is already among the US' top multifamily and residential mortgage lenders, this is the biggest investment it has ever made in homebuilding initiatives. "Housing, you have two issues: One is affordable, so we're doing a lot of affordable housing," Dimon told CNBC on August 5. "The other one is supply. Supply is mostly around permitting, approvals, local zoning requirements." It's part of a larger phenomenon. Banks are partnering with developers to help cities build multifamily developments — like apartment buildings — from the very beginning. And it could benefit both banks, which are encouraged through various government programs to make these kinds of community investments, and residents in expensive cities seeking an affordable home. A slew of banks have committed to affordable housing financing Building enough houses and apartments to meet America's demand isn't cheap. In New York City, for example, Mayor Zohran Mamdani's pledge to build 200,000 new affordable homes is slated to cost $22 billion in capital investment over five years. Governments and independent developers in NYC, San Francisco, Atlanta, and more have called on banks to help fund housing projects. Wall Street giants often back affordable housing ventures, alongside philanthropists and local governments. Business Insider recently toured a Midtown Manhattan hotel-to-apartment conversion that's being partially funded by Wells Fargo and JPMorgan Chase, as well as an affordable housing development for seniors in Brooklyn that was partially backed by TD Bank. Local property developer David Schwartz previously told Business Insider that this support is especially necessary for affordable housing. Land, construction, and architecture costs are the same as any other space, but long-term tenant returns are lower than in market-rate or luxury buildings. "That's the challenge," he said. While banks have long had a hand in real estate, their investment in affordable housing developments is gaining momentum. Bank of America provided upwards of $42 billion in financing for affordable housing efforts between 2020 and 2025, and Citi committed $60 billion to housing affordability efforts between 2026 and the early 2030s. This comes as the US' affordable housing supply continues to lag demand, and the rental vacancy rate is climbing because many lower- and middle-income households can't afford to pay the market rate. For residents, bank investment in housing could be good news. JPMorgan said roughly $200 million of its multibillion-dollar investment will be directed toward affordable developments in San Francisco, which Dimon has expressed specific concern about as one of America's priciest markets. Olivia Barrow Strauss, vice president of housing at the JPMorgan Chase Policy Center, told Business Insider that funding must go hand in hand with strong policy. "That includes modernizing zoning and permitting, unlocking underused land, and strengthening public-private partnerships so more housing can move from concept to construction," she said. Because "capital alone won't solve the country's housing affordability challenges." Banks and cities could both benefit What's in it for the banks? Investing in affordable homes is a potential path to tax breaks and economic development. The federal government offers a low-income housing tax credit to investors and developers who build or rehabilitate affordable housing, and a new markets tax credit to incentivize investment in low-income and distressed communities. Parties can then claim an annual tax break — so long as a portion of the apartments is set aside for low- and middle-income residents or materially improves residents' lives in eligible areas. Credits like this are sometimes distributed at the state and local level, and banks might be able to write off their assistance for first-time homebuyers. Citi has published disclosures that it "may employ a combination of taxable and tax-exempt loans or bonds, a combination of taxable and tax-exempt loans or bonds; Low Income, Historic or New Markets Tax Credits; and government and private subsidies," as part of its housing plan. Bank of America made similar statements in regulatory filings. It's unclear exactly which subsidies JPMorgan Chase qualifies for, and how much the bank's annual tax break will be, but government credits are likely a factor in its $750 billion investment. "Tax credits and subsidies are important tools to encourage public and private investments that create or preserve affordable housing because they can help close financing gaps," Karen Purcell, head of Community Development Banking at JPMorgan Chase, told Business Insider. Still, these credits aren't a cure-all, she said, "and often don't reach the 'missing middle,' which is why moderate-income housing remains chronically undersupplied." Passed in the 1970s, the Community Reinvestment Act also requires banks to provide financial support to the communities where they operate, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods. Backing affordable housing developments and providing resources to homebuyers are ways banks can comply with this law. CRA requires banks to publish their performance review. Between 2020 and 2023, JPMorgan Chase's disclosures show the bank scored "outstanding" in 31 of the 56 lending areas — criteria that's based on both the bank's lending behavior and the demographics it served. The public sector is making big bets on affordable housing , too. Congress passed a bipartisan housing bill in July. The law is set to loosen zoning restrictions, boost resources for communities impacted by natural disasters, and make it harder for major corporations to buy residential real estate. Big bank investment won't be capped by this law, and it may create more opportunities for public-private affordable housing ventures in the future. As Dimon put it to CNBC, "The bill the House passed is a very good bill, and then we have to do complements to it locally." Read the original article on Business Insider
